statement: The Roman invasion of Africa lasted from 204 to 201 BC.
A Roman army under Publius Cornelius Scipio landed near Utica in 204 BC.
The Roman army under Publius Cornelius Scipio decisively defeated the Carthaginian Empire.
The defeat of the Carthaginian Empire ended the Second Punic War.
The First Punic War was fought between Carthage and Rome for 23 years, from 264 to 241 BC.
After a 23-year interbellum, war broke out again in 218 BC.
The war was marked by Hannibal's campaign in Italy.
Scipio was Rome's most successful commander.
Scipio was assigned to Sicily with the intention of invading the Carthaginian homeland in North Africa.
Scipio's army landed in North Africa in 204 BC.
Scipio's army pillaged a large area.
Scipio's army laid siege to the port-city of Utica.
Scipio intended to use Utica as a permanent base.
Scipio intended to use Utica as a harbour proof against the winter weather.
A large Carthaginian army, supported by a larger force of allied Numidians, set up camp 11 kilometres (7 mi) south of Utica.
This caused the Romans to break off the siege and withdraw into their own camp for the winter.
In the spring of 203 BC, Scipio feigned that he was renewing the siege of Utica.
Scipio launched night attacks on the enemy camps in the spring of 203 BC.
Scipio's night attacks wiped out both armies.
The Carthaginian army reassembled 120 kilometres (75 mi) from Utica.
The Romans marched to meet the reassembled Carthaginian army.
The Romans left the siege largely in the hands of the navy.
At the battle of the Great Plains the Carthaginians were again badly beaten.
A large Carthaginian-supporting force of Numidians retreated towards their capital, Cirta.
They were pursued by an army of Roman-aligned Numidians supported by a Roman cadre.
The Romans won the subsequent battle of Cirta.
The Romans captured the city of Cirta.
After the Great Plains, the majority of the Roman army marched on Tunis.
Tunis was only 24 kilometres (15 mi) from the city of Carthage.
Shortly after, the Carthaginian fleet sailed from Carthage to relieve Utica.
When the Carthaginian fleet arrived, it found that the Roman fleet had adopted a novel formation.
The Carthaginian fleet was unable to fully overcome the Roman fleet's novel formation.
The Carthaginian fleet retreated after a day's fighting.
The Carthaginian Senate recalled Hannibal from Italy.
The Carthaginian Senate entered into peace negotiations with Scipio to end the war.
A draft treaty was agreed.
The Roman Senate ratified the draft treaty.
Carthage repudiated the draft treaty in early 202 BC.
Carthage repudiated the treaty because of mistrust and a surge in confidence when Hannibal arrived from Italy.
Hannibal set out to engage Scipio.
Hannibal's army was annihilated after the protracted and hard-fought battle of Zama.
The Carthaginians sued for peace.
The Romans enforced harsh terms in the subsequent peace treaty.
The peace treaty was agreed in 201 BC.
The Romans did leave North Africa.
Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome thereafter.
The main source for almost every aspect of the Punic Wars is the historian Polybius.
Polybius lived from approximately 200 to 118 BC.
Polybius was a Greek.
Polybius was sent to Rome in 167 BC as a hostage.
Polybius's works include a now largely lost manual on military tactics.
Polybius is best known for The Histories.
The Histories was written sometime after 146 BC.
Polybius's work is considered broadly objective and largely neutral as between Carthaginian and Roman points of view.
Polybius was an analytical historian.
Polybius interviewed participants from both sides in the events he wrote about wherever possible.
The accuracy of Polybius's account has been much debated over the past 150 years.
The modern consensus is to accept Polybius's account largely at face value.
The details of the war in modern sources are largely based on interpretations of Polybius's account.
The modern historian Andrew Curry sees Polybius as being "fairly reliable".
Craige Champion describes Polybius as "a remarkably well-informed, industrious, and insightful historian".
Much of Polybius's account of the Second Punic War is missing, or only exists in fragmentary form.
The account of the Roman historian Livy relied heavily on Polybius.
Livy's account is used by modern historians where Polybius's account is not extant.
The classicist Adrian Goldsworthy says Livy's "reliability is often suspect".
The historian Philip Sabin refers to Livy's "military ignorance".
Dexter Hoyos describes Livy's account of the battle of Zama as "bizarrely at odds with Polybius' which he seems not to understand fully".
Other, later, ancient histories of the war exist, although often in fragmentary or summary form.
Modern historians usually take into account the writings of Appian and Cassius Dio.
Appian and Cassius Dio were two Greek authors.
Appian and Cassius Dio wrote during the Roman era.
Appian and Cassius Dio are described by John Lazenby as "clearly far inferior" to Livy.
Some otherwise-lost fragments of Polybius can be recovered from their texts.
The Greek moralist Plutarch wrote several biographies of Roman commanders in his Parallel Lives.
Other sources include coins, inscriptions, archaeological evidence and empirical evidence from reconstructions.
The First Punic War was fought between Carthage and Rome.
Carthage and Rome were the two main powers of the western Mediterranean in the 3rd century BC.
Carthage and Rome struggled for supremacy primarily on the Mediterranean island of Sicily and its surrounding waters.
Carthage and Rome struggled for supremacy also in North Africa.
The war lasted for 23 years.
The war lasted from 264 to 241 BC.
The Carthaginians were defeated in the war.
Under the Treaty of Lutatius, Carthage evacuated Sicily.
Under the Treaty of Lutatius, Carthage paid Rome an indemnity of 3,200 silver talents over ten years.
Four years later, Rome seized Sardinia and Corsica.
Rome seized Sardinia and Corsica on a cynical pretence.
Rome imposed a further 1,200 talent indemnity.
These actions fuelled Carthaginian resentment.
Polybius considered this act of bad faith by the Romans to be the single greatest cause of war with Carthage breaking out again nineteen years later.
In 236 BC, an army commanded by Hamilcar Barca landed in Carthaginian Iberia.
Hamilcar Barca was the leading Carthaginian general.
Carthaginian Iberia is now part of southeast Spain and Portugal.
Carthaginian Iberia became a quasi-monarchial, autonomous territory ruled by the Barcids.
The expansion gained Carthage silver mines.
The expansion gained Carthage agricultural wealth.
The expansion gained Carthage manpower.
The expansion gained Carthage military facilities such as shipyards.
The expansion gained Carthage territorial depth.
The expansion enabled Carthage to resist future Roman demands.
Hamilcar ruled as viceroy until his death in 228 BC.
Hamilcar was succeeded by his son-in-law, Hasdrubal, in 228 BC.
Hasdrubal was succeeded by Hamilcar's son Hannibal in 221 BC.
In 226 BC, the Ebro Treaty established the Ebro River as the northern boundary of the Carthaginian sphere of influence.
Rome made a separate treaty of association with the city of Saguntum, well south of the Ebro.
In 218 BC, a Carthaginian army under Hannibal besieged Saguntum.
In 218 BC, a Carthaginian army under Hannibal captured Saguntum.
In 218 BC, a Carthaginian army under Hannibal sacked Saguntum.
In early 219 BC Rome declared war on Carthage.
Hannibal led a large Carthaginian army from Iberia, through Gaul, over the Alps and invaded mainland Italy.
During the next three years Hannibal inflicted heavy defeats on the Romans at the battles of the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae.
At the battle of Cannae alone, at least 67,500 Romans were killed or captured.
The historian Toni Ñaco del Hoyo describes these as "great military calamities".
Brian Carey writes that they brought Rome to the brink of collapse.
Hannibal's army campaigned in Italy for 14 years before the survivors withdrew.
There was also extensive fighting in Iberia (modern Spain and Portugal), Sicily, Sardinia and North Africa.
In 211 BC, the Romans suffered a severe reverse at the battle of the Upper Baetis.
The Romans were penned back by the Carthaginians to the north-east corner of Iberia in 211 BC.
In 210 BC Roman reinforcements stabilised the situation.
Later that year Publius Cornelius Scipio arrived with further Roman reinforcements to take command in Iberia.
In a carefully planned assault in 209 BC, Scipio captured the lightly defended centre of Carthaginian power in Iberia, New Carthage.
During the following four years, Scipio repeatedly defeated the Carthaginians.
Scipio drove the Carthaginians out of Iberia in 205 BC.
Most male Roman citizens were eligible for military service.
Most male Roman citizens would serve as infantry.
A better-off minority of Roman citizens provided a cavalry component.
Traditionally, when at war the Romans would raise two legions, each of 4,200 infantry and 300 cavalry.
Approximately 1,200 of the infantry served as javelin-armed skirmishers known as velites.
These velites were poorer or younger men.
These velites were unable to afford the armour and equipment of a standard legionary.
Velites each carried several javelins.
Javelins would be thrown from a distance.
Velites carried a short sword.
Velites carried a 90-centimetre (3 ft) shield.
The balance of the infantry were equipped as heavy infantry, with body armour, a large shield and short thrusting swords.
Heavy infantry were divided into three ranks.
The front rank carried two javelins.
The second and third ranks had a thrusting spear.
Both legionary sub-units and individual legionaries fought in relatively open order.
It was the long-standing Roman procedure to elect two men each year as senior magistrates, known as consuls.
Consuls would each lead an army in time of war.
An army was usually formed by combining a Roman legion with a similarly sized and equipped legion provided by their Latin allies.
Allied legions usually had a larger attached complement of cavalry than Roman ones.
By this stage of the war, Roman armies were generally larger.
Roman armies typically consisted of four legions, two Roman and two provided by its allies, for a total of approximately 20,000 men.
The Roman army which invaded Africa consisted of the now standard four legions.
The Roman pair of legions were each reinforced to an unprecedented 6,200 infantry.
The Roman pair of legions had the more usual 300 cavalry.
Modern historians estimate the army to have totalled 25,000–35,000 men, including perhaps 2,500 cavalry.
Carthaginian citizens only served in their army if there was a direct threat to the city of Carthage.
When they did, Carthaginian citizens fought as well-armoured heavy infantry armed with long thrusting spears.
Carthaginian citizens were notoriously ill-trained and ill-disciplined.
In most circumstances Carthage recruited non-citizens to make up its army.
Many non-citizens recruited by Carthage were from North Africa.
These non-citizens were frequently referred to as "Libyans".
The region provided close order infantry equipped with large shields, helmets, short swords and long thrusting spears.
The region provided javelin-armed light infantry skirmishers.
The region provided close order shock cavalry (also known as "heavy cavalry") carrying spears.
The region provided light cavalry skirmishers who threw javelins from a distance and avoided close combat.
Light cavalry skirmishers were usually Numidians.
Many of the African light infantry were Numidians.
The close order African infantry and the citizen-militia both fought in a tightly-packed formation known as a phalanx.
The Carthaginians also employed war elephants.
North Africa had indigenous African forest elephants at the time.
Both Iberia and Gaul provided many experienced infantry and cavalry.
The infantry from these areas were unarmoured troops who would charge ferociously.
The infantry from these areas had a reputation for breaking off if a combat was protracted.
The Gallic cavalry wore armour.
The Gallic cavalry fought as close order troops.
Possibly some of the Iberians wore armour and fought as close order troops.
Most or all of the mounted Iberians were light cavalry.
Slingers were frequently recruited from the Balearic Islands.
The Carthaginians relied on the troop types mentioned above to make up their armies which participated in the campaigns of 204 and 203 BC.
The proportions and numbers of the different troop types in these armies are not known.
4,000 freshly recruited Iberian warriors took part in the battle of the Great Plains in 203 BC.

The competing Numidian forces which supported both the Carthaginians and the Romans consisted predominately or entirely of their javelin-armed light cavalry and infantry, with a high proportion of cavalry.
The campaign of 202 BC climaxed in the battle of Zama.
The Carthaginians were reinforced by the armies of Hannibal and Mago for the campaign of 202 BC.
Hannibal and Mago had been campaigning in southern and north-west Italy respectively until recalled.
An unclear number of troops were raised in Africa.
A contingent of Ligurian came from north Italy.
Among Hannibal's veterans were many Bruttians from the south west.
Both Ligurian and Bruttian troops fought as heavy infantry.
In 206 BC, Scipio left Iberia after four years.
Scipio returned to Italy in 206 BC.
Scipio was denied the triumph that he would normally have expected.
Scipio was denied the triumph on the grounds that he had not occupied any of the magistracies of the cursus honorum.
The cursus honorum was the sequential mixture of military and political administrative positions held by aspiring Roman politicians.
Scipio was elected to the senior position of consul in early 205 BC.
Scipio did not meet the age requirement for consul.
Scipio was already anticipating an invasion of North Africa.
While still in Spain, Scipio had been negotiating with the Numidian leaders Masinissa and Syphax.
Scipio failed to win over Syphax.
Scipio made an ally of Masinissa.
Opinion was divided in Roman political circles as to whether an invasion of North Africa was excessively risky.
Hannibal was still on Italian soil.
There was the possibility of further Carthaginian invasions.
Mago Barca landed in Liguria.
The practical difficulties of an amphibious invasion and its logistical follow-up were considerable.
The Romans had invaded North Africa in 256 BC during the First Punic War.
The Romans had been driven out with heavy losses.
The Roman defeat had re-energised the Carthaginians.
Eventually a compromise was agreed.
Scipio was given Sicily as his consular province.
Sicily was the best location for the Romans to launch an invasion of the Carthaginian homeland from.
Sicily was the best location for the Romans to logistically support an invasion of the Carthaginian homeland.
Roman commitment was less than whole hearted.
Scipio could not conscript troops for his consular army.
Scipio could only call for volunteers for his consular army.
Conscripting troops for a consular army was usual.
In 216 BC, the survivors of the Roman defeat at the Battle of Cannae had been formed into two legions.
The survivors were sent to Sicily as a punishment.
The survivors still formed the main part of the garrison of Sicily.
Scipio used his volunteers to increase the strength of each of these legions to an unprecedented 6,500.
The total number of men available to Scipio and how many of them travelled to Africa is unclear.
Livy gives totals for the invasion force of either 12,200, 17,600 or 35,000.
Modern historians estimate a combat strength of 25,000–30,000 for the invasion force.
More than 90% of the estimated combat strength were infantry.
Up to half of the complement of Scipio's legions were fresh volunteers.
No fighting had taken place on Sicily for the past five years.
Scipio instigated a rigorous training regime.
The training regime ranged from drill by individual centuries to exercises by the full army.
A century was the basic Roman army manoeuvre unit of 80 men.
These training regimes lasted for approximately a year.
At the same time the Romans assembled a vast quantity of food.
Scipio intended to largely feed his army from stockpiles in Sicily, Sardinia and southern Italy.
This intention was to free the army from the need to forage.
War materiel was prepared in great quantities.
Merchant ships to transport materiel and troops were built.
Warships to escort the transports were built.
Crews were trained.
During 205 BC, thirty Roman ships under Gaius Laelius raided North Africa around Hippo Regius.
Gaius Laelius was Scipio's second-in-command.
The raid gathered large quantities of loot.
The raid gathered large numbers of captives.
The Carthaginians initially believed that this was the anticipated invasion by Scipio and his full invasion force.
The Carthaginians hastily strengthened fortifications.
The Carthaginians raised troops, including some units made up of Carthaginian citizens.
Reinforcements were sent to Mago in an attempt to distract the Romans in Italy.
A succession war had broken out in Numidia between the Roman-supporting Masinissa and the Carthaginian-inclined Syphax.
Laelius re-established contact with Masinissa during his raid.
Masinissa expressed dismay at how long it was taking the Romans to complete their preparations and land in Africa.
In 204 BC, probably in June or July, the Roman army left Sicily in 400 transport ships.
The Roman army was escorted by 40 galleys.
Three days later, they disembarked at Cape Farina 20 kilometres (12 mi) north of the large Carthaginian port of Utica.
The ships which had landed the Roman army returned to Sicily to pick up supplies.
Scipio wished to build up a stock of food and water for forty-five days.
A third of the food was already cooked, as bread or biscuit.
The locals fled.
Carthage's immediate response, a scouting party of 500 cavalry, was defeated.
The scouting party suffered the loss of its commander and the general in overall charge of responding to the invasion.
The area was pillaged.
8,000 captives were taken, to be sent back to Sicily as slaves.
A large fortified camp was established at Ghar el-Melh which was known as Castra Cornelia.
Masinissa had been recently defeated by his Numidian rival Syphax.
Masinissa was wounded.
Masinissa had his army scattered.
Syphax had been persuaded to take firm action by the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal Gisco.
Syphax had been persuaded to take firm action by his assertive new wife, Hasdrubal's daughter Sophonisba.
Masinissa joined the Romans with either 200 or 2,000 men.
The sources differ on the number of men Masinissa joined the Romans with.
Carthage sent a larger party to probe the Roman position, about 4,000 soldiers under a general called Hanno.
Hanno's command of mixed Numidians and Carthaginian citizens based itself at Salaeca, 24 kilometres (15 mi) from the Romans.
Hanno's command did little scouting.
Following a stratagem agreed with Scipio, Masinissa's cavalry raided Hanno's force.
Hanno's force chased Masinissa's cavalry off.
Hanno's force pursued Masinissa's cavalry into a Roman ambush.
Hanno and 1,000 of his men were killed or taken prisoner.
The survivors were in turn pursued for 50 kilometres (30 mi).
Only 1,000 escaped.
The Romans pillaged an ever-wider area.
The Romans sent their loot and prisoners to Sicily in the ships bringing their supplies.
Granaries were constructed at Castra Cornelia to hold the supplies of food and materiel.
The sources mention a delivery of 1,200 togas and 12,000 tunics.
Scipio besieged Utica, wanting a more permanent base.
Scipio wanted a port more resilient to the bad weather to be expected when winter came.
The siege dragged on into the winter.
A Carthaginian army under Hasdrubal set up a fortified camp 11 kilometres (7 mi) from the Romans with a reported 33,000 men.
Syphax joined Hasdrubal, establishing his own camp a mile (2 km) away with a reported 60,000 troops.
The large size of both of these armies as reported by ancient historians have been questioned by their modern counterparts.
It is accepted that the Romans were considerably outnumbered, in particular in terms of cavalry.
The Romans were besieging Utica.
The Romans were themselves now blockaded on the landward side.
The Carthaginian camp was solidly constructed, with timber-built barracks.
The Numidian camp was less solidly constructed.
The accommodation for the Numidian soldiers was largely constructed of, and roofed with, reeds.
Scipio sent emissaries to Syphax to attempt to persuade him to defect.
Syphax in turn offered to broker peace terms.
A series of exchanges of negotiating parties followed.
With his delegations, Scipio sent junior officers disguised as slaves to report back on the layout and construction of the Numidian camp.
Scipio drew out the negotiations with Syphax.
Scipio stated that he was in broad agreement with the proposition, but that his senior officers were not yet convinced.
As the better weather of spring approached, Scipio made an announcement to his troops that he would shortly attempt to storm the defences of Utica.
Scipio began preparations to storm the defences of Utica.
Simultaneously, Scipio was planning a night attack on both camps.
Local knowledge and careful scouting identified the routes least likely to cause problems at night.
Scipio briefed his senior officers carefully.
On the night of the attack, two columns set out.
One column was commanded by Gaius Laelius, a legate and the Roman army's second in command.
Gaius Laelius had years of experience of operating under Scipio.
This force consisted of about half the Romans and was accompanied by the Numidians.
Its target was Syphax's camp.
Scipio led the balance of the Roman force against the Carthaginian camp.
Thanks to the careful prior reconnoitring, both forces reached the positions from which they were to start their attacks without issue.
Masinissa's Numidian cavalry positioned themselves in small groups so as to cover every route out of the two enemy camps.
Laelius's column attacked first.
Laelius's column stormed the camp of Syphax's Numidians.
Laelius's column concentrated on setting fire to as many of the reed huts as possible.
The camp dissolved into chaos.
Many of its Numidian occupants were oblivious of the Roman attack.
Many of its Numidian occupants thought that the barracks had caught fire accidentally.
The Carthaginians heard the commotion and saw the blaze.
Some of the Carthaginians set off to help extinguish the fire.
With pre-planned coordination, Scipio's contingent then attacked.
They cut down the Carthaginians heading for their ally's camp.
They stormed Hasdrubal's camp.
They attempted to set fire to the wooden housing.
The fire spread between the close-spaced barracks.
Carthaginians rushed out into the dark and confusion, without armour or weapons, either trying to escape the flames or to fight the fire.
The organised and prepared Romans cut them down.
Polybius writes that Hasdrubal escaped from his burning camp with only 2,500 men.
Numidian losses are not recorded.
By the diplomatic standards of the time, Scipio launching a surprise attack while in the midst of peace negotiations was ethically dubious.
With no Carthaginian field army to threaten them, the Romans pressed their siege of Utica.
The Romans pillaged an extensive area of North Africa with large and far-ranging raids.
As well as gold and slaves, the Romans accumulated large amounts of foodstuffs.
This was added to the stocks already built up by shipping grain from Sicily.
When word of the defeat reached Carthage there was panic.
Some in Carthage wanted to renew the peace negotiations.
The Carthaginian Senate also heard demands for Hannibal's army to be recalled.
A decision was reached to fight on with locally available resources.
A force of 4,000 Iberian warriors arrived in Carthage.
Their strength was exaggerated to 10,000 to maintain morale.
Hasdrubal raised further local troops with whom to reinforce the survivors of Utica.
Syphax remained loyal and joined Hasdrubal with what was left of his army.
The combined force is estimated at 30,000.
They established a strong camp on a flat plain by the Bagradas River known as the Great Plains.
The camp was established within 30–50 days of the defeat at Utica.
This was near modern Souk el Kremis and about 120 kilometres (75 mi) from Utica.
Hearing of this, Scipio immediately marched most of his men to the scene.
The size of Scipio's army is not known.
It is agreed that Scipio's army was outnumbered by the Carthaginians.
A sufficient force was left to hold the Roman camps and to continue the siege of Utica.
After several days of skirmishing both armies committed to a pitched battle.
Upon being charged by the Romans and Masinissa's Numidians, all of those Carthaginians who had been involved in the debacle at Utica turned and fled.
Morale had not recovered among the Carthaginians.
Only the Iberians stood and fought.
The Iberians were enveloped by the well-drilled Roman legions and wiped out.
Hasdrubal fled to Carthage.
Hasdrubal was demoted and exiled in Carthage.
The majority of the Romans remained in the area under Scipio.
The Romans devastated the countryside and captured and sacked many towns.
They then moved to Tunis, which had been abandoned by the Carthaginians.
Tunis was only 24 kilometres (15 mi) from the city of Carthage.
This cut Carthage off from its hinterland.
After the battle of the Great Plains, Masinissa's Numidians pursued their defeated countrymen under Syphax.
Masinissa's Numidians were accompanied by part of the Roman force, under Laelius.
Syphax withdrew as far as his capital, Cirta.
Syphax recruited more troops to supplement those survivors who had stayed with him on the retreat from the Great Plains.
This force commenced an intensive training regime.
Masinissa and Laelius's men took 15 days to reach Masinissa's ancestral lands, those of the Massyli.
The historian Peter Edwell comments that venturing so far into the interior was a high-risk enterprise.
Masinissa was proclaimed king.
Syphax's administrators and garrisons were expelled.
Not wanting to allow Syphax to train his new troops up, Masinissa and Laelius pressed on towards Cirta.
Syphax determined to oppose the allied army immediately.
They met at the battle of Cirta.
The battle of Cirta started as a sprawling cavalry engagement.
Each side sent detachments to hurl javelins at the other and then withdrawing.
Having more cavalry, Syphax's army gained the upper hand.
Laelius then inserted groups of Roman light infantry between Masinissa's cavalry detachments.
These men were able to hold off the enemy cavalry and form an approximate battle line.
The Roman heavy infantry were then able to advance.
Seeing these legionaries advancing to join the battle, Syphax's troops broke and fled.
Syphax attempted to rally his men.
Syphax's horse was shot.
Syphax was thrown and captured.
Many of Syphax's defeated and demoralised troops fled back to Cirta.
Masinissa pursued them with the cavalry.
Laelius followed with the infantry.
After Syphax was paraded beneath the city walls in chains, Cirta surrendered to Masinissa.
Masinissa then took over much of Syphax's kingdom and joined it to his own.
Syphax was taken as a prisoner to Italy, where he died.
Over the winter the Carthaginians had increased the number of equipped and crewed war galleys they had.
The Carthaginians felt ready to challenge the Romans at sea.
At some point while the Roman army was in Tunis, the Carthaginian fleet left port and sailed for Utica.
The Carthaginian fleet intended to lift the siege and hoped to wipe out the Roman fleet while doing so.
Utica is only 56 kilometres (35 mi) north of Carthage.
The Carthaginian ships did not arrive until the next morning.
Overnight the Romans had expediently lashed the whole of their fleet into one unit.
The Roman fleet had several ranks of transports in front of the specialist war galleys.
On the foremost row of transports were 1,000 soldiers with a large supply of javelins.
The Carthaginian fleet attacked shortly after sunrise.
The improvised Roman formation frustrated the Carthaginian fleet.
They faced a tight-locked wall of transports.
The transports' higher freeboard meant the Carthaginians had to improvise grappling hooks or ladders to board them.
The Roman marines could hurl javelins down onto the open decks of the Carthaginian galleys from relatively protected positions.
By the end of the day the Carthaginians had managed to capture, cut loose, and tow away 60 Roman transports.
They made their way back to Carthage with their captives.
The Carthaginians left the majority of the transports and all of the Roman war galleys unscathed.
The Carthaginian Senate recalled both Hannibal and Mago from Italy.
The Carthaginian Senate entered into peace discussions with Scipio to end the war.
Scipio demanded the handing over of all prisoners and deserters.
Scipio demanded Carthaginian withdrawal from Italy and Spain.
Scipio demanded the handing over of their entire navy bar a coastal defence force.
Scipio demanded the supply of a vast amount of grain to the Romans.
Scipio demanded the payment of 5,000 talents as an indemnity.
The Carthaginians considered themselves to be in a desperate situation.
The Carthaginians accepted the demanding terms Scipio put forward with little attempt at negotiation.
The Roman Senate ratified the draft treaty.
Carthage repudiated the treaty in early 202 BC because of mistrust and a surge in confidence when Hannibal arrived from Italy.
Hannibal was placed in command of another army.
The army was formed of his and Mago's veterans from Italy and newly raised troops from Africa.
The army had 80 war elephants but few cavalry.
The decisive Battle of Zama followed in October 202 BC.
Hannibal was supported by 2,000 Numidian cavalry commanded by a relative of Syphax's, Tychaeus.
Masinissa fought alongside the Romans with 6,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry.
Hannibal attempted to use the elephants to break into the Roman infantry formation.
The Romans countered the elephants effectively.
The elephants routed back through the Carthaginian ranks.
The Roman and allied Numidian cavalry then attacked the Carthaginian cavalry.
The Roman and allied Numidian cavalry drove the Carthaginian cavalry from the field and pursued them.
The two sides' infantry fought fiercely but inconclusively.
The Roman and Numidian cavalry returned and attacked the Carthaginian rear.
The Carthaginian formation collapsed.
Hannibal was one of the few to escape.
After the Romans had returned to Utica, Scipio received word that a Numidian army under Syphax's son Vermina was marching to Carthage's assistance.
This army was intercepted and surrounded by a Roman force largely made up of cavalry.
The Numidian army was defeated.
The number of Numidians involved is not known.
Livy records that more than 16,000 Numidians were killed or captured.
This was the last battle of the Second Punic War.
With the Carthaginians completely defeated, the peace treaty the Romans subsequently imposed on them was harsh.
The treaty stripped Carthage of all of its non-African territories and some of its African ones.
An indemnity of 10,000 silver talents was to be paid over 50 years.
Hostages were taken from Carthage.
Carthage was forbidden to possess war elephants.
Carthage's fleet was restricted to 10 warships.
Carthage was prohibited from waging war outside Africa.
Carthage was prohibited from waging war in Africa only with Rome's express permission.
Many senior Carthaginians wanted to reject the treaty.
Hannibal spoke strongly in its favour.
The treaty was accepted in spring 201 BC.
Henceforth, it was clear Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome.
Scipio was awarded a triumph.
Scipio received the agnomen "Africanus".
Masinissa established himself as the senior ruler in Numidia.
Masinissa exploited the prohibition on Carthage waging war to repeatedly raid and seize Carthaginian territory with impunity.
Carthage appealed to Rome.
Rome always backed their Numidian ally.
In 149 BC, fifty years after the end of the Second Punic War, Carthage sent an army, under Hasdrubal the Boeotarch, against Masinissa.
The campaign ended in disaster at the battle of Oroscopa.
Anti-Carthaginian factions in Rome used the illicit military action as a pretext to prepare a punitive expedition.
The Third Punic War began later in 149 BC.
A large Roman army landed in North Africa and besieged Carthage in 149 BC.
In the spring of 146 BC the Romans launched their final assault.
The Romans systematically destroyed the city and killed its inhabitants.
50,000 survivors were sold into slavery.
The formerly Carthaginian territories became the Roman province of Africa.
It was a century before the site of Carthage was rebuilt as a Roman city.
